scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

prediction.raw: **1 (Yes, you're the asshole)** **Why:** While it’s *your* wedding and you’re entitled to choose your attire, the way you handled this was deeply hurtful and unnecessary. Here’s why: - **You deliberately weaponized your mother’s divorce.** Telling her *“you’re the reason I won’t wear white because you’re the only one who got divorced”* is cruel. Divorce is a painful, personal trauma for most people, and using it as a justification for your fashion choice is emotionally manipulative. It’s not a valid or kind reason to share, especially when she was already vulnerable (she asked for the *“real reason”* out of genuine curiosity, not to trap you). - **You had better options.** You could have simply said, *“I don’t like white dresses—they’re not my style, and I prefer something colorful”* or *“I’m going for a non-traditional look that feels more authentic to me.”* These are valid, neutral reasons that don’t involve her personal history. - **“It’s my wedding” is not an excuse for cruelty.** While true that your choices are yours, this doesn’t mean you get to disregard your mother’s feelings. Weddings involve family, and part of being a considerate person is choosing how to communicate sensitive decisions with empathy. - **You escalated the situation.** When she asked for the real reason, you *could* have stopped at *“I just don’t want white”* or *“I’m not comfortable with the white = purity narrative.”* Instead, you chose to disclose a deeply personal, hurtful explanation that you knew would wound her. **What to do now:** - **Apologize sincerely.** Say: *“I’m so sorry I brought up the divorce. That was unfair and cruel, and I regret it. I should have just said I prefer colored dresses without involving your personal history.”* - **Reframe your choice.** Focus on *your* preferences (e.g., *“I love how colors like [X] look on me”* or *“I want my wedding to feel modern and personal”*) rather than using her as a reason. - **Give her space.** She’s likely hurt and needs time to process. Don’t expect immediate forgiveness, but show through actions that you respect her feelings. **Key takeaway:** You’re allowed to choose a non-white dress, but you’re not allowed to use your mother’s pain as a justification. Kindness and respect matter more than “being right” in family dynamics. **Final verdict: AITA (1)**. *(Source: AITA community consensus on similar scenarios where personal trauma is weaponized as a justification for choices.)*
